entries.title: Gemini agents design cheaper quantum algorithms and prove them correct in Lean
entries.who: Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI
entries.system: Teams of Gemini 4 agents working in the Lean theorem prover
entries.sum: Agent teams wrote quantum programs against specifications that people stated in Lean, and Lean checked both that each program is correct and what it costs. The headline result is a routine for preparing an arcsin state whose estimated cost, measured as logical qubits times T gates, is about 290 times lower than a published design. The agents also cut estimated costs about 12-fold for a fusion stopping-power simulation, about 8-fold for a photochemistry simulation and about 2.5-fold for a drug-metabolism enzyme, and found up to 2.57 times fewer rounds for a multi-target Grover search.
entries.open: Not peer reviewed, and Google is the only source. Every figure is a resource estimate on paper, not a run on quantum hardware, and some baselines were adjusted by the authors. The paper does not say whether the Lean library has been released.

entries.title: OpenAI says its models redesigned parts of its own AI chip and found gains in AMD processor designs
entries.sum: OpenAI says changes its models proposed for Jalapeño, its first in-house inference chip, shrank the logic area of the vector unit by about 13% and the matrix unit by about 10%, and that these changes worked in the finished silicon. One redesigned multiplier used about 15% less area and finished in one clock cycle instead of two. On AMD's flagship GPU designs the models found power, performance and area gains of up to 14% over heavily tuned baselines, and some of those changes are in a chip AMD has sent for manufacturing.
entries.open: OpenAI is the only source, and AMD is not quoted. The baselines are not disclosed, the Jalapeño area figures come from synthesis rather than final layout, and no test results have been reported for the AMD chip.

entries.title: Mathematician says he and Claude have proved the Riemann hypothesis, and posts only Lean code
entries.sum: In a four-page note posted on November 20, Levent Alpöge says that, working with Claude, he found a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the 1859 conjecture about how prime numbers are spread out, and that the method also settles the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. He has released only a Lean formalization, split into 14 archive files, because he says a written version runs past 250,000 pages. He credits Claude with key steps near the end, including the idea of chaining theta lifts about the square root of X times.
entries.open: The Lean check is now strong: the Lean and Mathlib communities issued a joint statement saying they are fully confident the proof is correct, after MIT's Andrew Sutherland recompiled it on the kernel's three standard axioms and a comparator run found no redefined terms in the statement. What is still missing is mathematics people can read: there is no written paper, no peer review, and Alpöge says a shorter human version will take months. A separate, all-human draft proof by Alessandro Masullo, reviewed for months by Stanford's Brian Conrad, was posted by Ravi Vakil the same day; mathematicians have flagged problems in it and it is not yet accepted.

entries.title: Claude agents settle two open problems in black hole physics
entries.who: Anthropic (project set up by researcher Hongbin Chen)
entries.sum: Anthropic says Claude agents finished a calculation set up in 2003 but never completed, showing that a transition in a simplified model universe is abrupt, as Hawking and Page predicted for black holes. A second result raises a long-standing bound in the modular bootstrap from about 8.5 to about 9.13, which Anthropic says is the best possible. Independent agents redid nearly every step, a physicist checked the main results, and Anthropic says the bootstrap result was verified in Lean.
entries.open: Anthropic is the main source. Both preprints are unreviewed, list no human authors and are labelled primarily AI-generated. Anthropic says neither result describes our universe or has practical use.

entries.title: GPT-6 Astra credited with the proof behind a candidate lattice definition of the Standard Model
entries.who: Nathaniel Craig (UC Santa Barbara, visiting scientist at OpenAI)
entries.sum: Putting the Standard Model on a spacetime grid has been stuck for decades because the weak force treats left- and right-handed particles differently, and Lüscher's fix for simpler theories had not been carried over to the full model in more than 25 years. Craig says he had a strategy but could not prove it in every case, and that Astra turned it into a construction and led the detailed proof. The preprint, posted October 6, builds a gauge-invariant fermion measure on four-dimensional lattices for a class of theories that includes the Standard Model, and comes with a Lean 4 formalization.
entries.open: The model's role rests on Craig's own account, published on OpenAI's science blog. Three lattice theorists read the work privately, but no outside assessment has been published. Reflection positivity and a link to a continuum theory are not established, and Craig calls it an answer in principle more than in practice.

entries.title: Gemini agents help prove the Courtade–Kumar conjecture, with a batch of new algorithm results
entries.who: Google Research with CUHK and other academic co-authors
entries.sum: The 2013 conjecture says no one-bit summary of a noisy signal carries more information than simply reading off a single input bit. Google says Gemini found counterexamples to a broader version, worked out most of the analytical bounds and interval-arithmetic certificates, and extended the proof from balanced to unbalanced functions without human input; the whole proof is formalized in about 50 million lines of Lean 4. The same post lists about ten further new results, including a deterministic Boolean matrix multiplication algorithm that answers an open question from STOC 2024 and the first n-bit functions needing more than n/2 quantum queries.
entries.open: Google and its co-authors are the only source, and nothing here has been peer reviewed or independently reproduced. People supplied key steps: the CUHK team proposed the function that cut the problem to a 14-variable optimization and gave one analytical bound. Google gives no count of problems attempted or failed.

entries.title: AI system proves the Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture on the limits of quantum speedups
entries.system: PSI research system running a non-public Anthropic model
entries.sum: The conjecture, open since 2008, says every bounded low-degree polynomial has at least one input bit with sizeable influence. PSI's system had a full proof by day three of its run and then tightened the bound twice, ending at an influence of at least about 0.0025·v^(5/2)/d^6 for variance v and degree d, where earlier bounds shrank exponentially with the degree. It follows that a quantum algorithm cannot save exponentially many input reads on typical random inputs to a yes/no problem.
entries.open: Not peer reviewed, and the model is not public. David Turturean posted the proof on arXiv on November 6, and four computer scientists led by Guy Blanc posted a reworked exposition on November 8; they say they worked to understand it, which is not a formal independent check. The result limits input reads, not total running time.

entries.title: Deep learning finds an ECG signal that flags sudden cardiac death risk
entries.sum: A model trained on Swedish heart tracings linked to death records picked out a pattern in ordinary ECGs that marks people at high risk of sudden cardiac death. The group it flagged died suddenly at about 7% a year, against 4.6% for the group picked by the standard pumping-strength test, and the pattern held in patient records from the US and Taiwan.
entries.open: Nobody yet knows what the signal is biologically, and it is not in clinical use.

entries.title: AlphaGenome 2 predicts what a DNA variant does in one chosen cell type
entries.sum: The model takes a stretch of DNA plus a tissue or cell state and predicts gene activity there. It recovered a known inflammatory bowel disease mechanism in gut macrophages and predicted that a variant tied to severe COVID-19 disrupts gene activity most in activated T cells.
entries.open: The findings are computational predictions that still need lab confirmation, and the announcement names no journal.

entries.title: AI agents formally verify the code behind Signal's encryption
entries.system: AlphaProof Code, agents on Gemini 4 Carbon
entries.sum: In about four weeks, agents wrote millions of lines of machine-checked Lean proof showing that the compiled Signal protocol code keeps its core security promises. When researchers put two old, already-fixed bugs back into a copy of the code, the system proved each buggy version insecure.
entries.open: A proof is only as good as its specification. Those were written and reviewed by people but have not had an outside audit, and no previously unknown bugs were reported.

entries.title: AI agents find two new weaknesses in retired RSA-1024 encryption
entries.who: Google DeepMind with UC San Diego and Inria
entries.sum: The agents found a signature-forgery shortcut that is up to 1,600 times faster on paper when an attacker controls only a small part of the signed data, and a batch method that cuts the cost of factoring each additional key about 30-fold.
entries.open: Both headline figures are theoretical or asymptotic, not measured attacks. Keys of 2048 bits and larger are unaffected.

entries.title: Proteins designed from plain-language descriptions work in the lab
entries.sum: Pinal turns a written description of a desired function into protein sequences. It produced working proteins on all four test tasks, a plastic-degrading enzyme among them, and one design lifted a carbon-fixation pathway to 1.7 times its natural output.
entries.open: Hit rates were uneven. One task yielded a single working protein from 29 tested.

entries.title: AI-designed antibody roughly doubles grip strength in mice with a muscular dystrophy
entries.sum: Anthropic reported a preclinical antibody for LAMA2-related muscular dystrophy that went from idea to mouse data in under 18 months. One design about doubled grip strength compared with untreated mice.
entries.open: This comes from a company technical report that has not been peer reviewed. Human trials are not expected before late 2028.

entries.title: OpenAI model claims the Exponential Time Hypothesis is false
entries.sum: The hypothesis says 3-SAT cannot be solved in sub-exponential time, and a large part of complexity theory is built on it. OpenAI says its model wrote a disproof on October 16 that was checked in Lean the next day. The paper and the formal proof are public.
entries.open: Outside experts are still working out whether the formal statement matches the claim and what the algorithm means in practice.

entries.title: OpenAI model claims a proof of local smoothing in every dimension
entries.sum: The local smoothing conjecture for the wave equation implies the Kakeya and restriction conjectures in harmonic analysis. OpenAI says its model proved it for all dimensions from two up on October 18, formalized it in Lean a day later, and published both on an expert's advice.
entries.open: Analysts have not yet confirmed the argument by hand.

entries.title: OpenAI reports a quantum chromodynamics result with a formalized Yang–Mills existence proof
entries.who: OpenAI, with a physics group led by David Gross
entries.sum: The third of three results announced together. OpenAI says the Yang–Mills existence part was formalized in Lean on October 16 and handed to a group of physicists for review.
entries.open: On November 9–10 the five-physicist group, which OpenAI chose, reported that the Lean code rebuilds cleanly and that its definitions match the standard statement of four-dimensional Yang–Mills existence, while saying it does not yet fully understand the proof. No fully independent check is on record, the 1,147-page written proof is still private, and the mass gap, the other half of the Millennium problem, is untouched. Critics including Peter Woit question whether the verified statement meets the prize problem's standard.

entries.title: OpenAI releases 722 AI-written manuscripts claiming hundreds of open problems
entries.sum: Posted to GitHub across 372 topics, the claims include a matrix multiplication exponent of 9/4, a proof of the unique games conjecture and a wide zero-free region for the Riemann zeta function. About half the manuscripts come with Lean proofs.
entries.open: Three papers were retracted and 14 revised within two days. Some formal proofs appear to establish less than the papers claim, and full review is expected to take months.

entries.title: OpenAI claims a solution to the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem
entries.system: Multi-agent system of roughly ten thousand agents
entries.sum: The company said its system settled existence and smoothness for the fluid equations with a smooth external force, one of the seven Millennium Prize problems.
entries.open: No complete independent check has been published. A paper by Bastounis, Circelli and Hansen argues that the Lean code does not correspond to the written blow-up proof, citing at least two discrepancies; that does not by itself show the proof is wrong, and no OpenAI fix is on record. Credit is also disputed: mathematician Tristan Buckmaster says unpublished results of his reached OpenAI days earlier.

entries.title: First working viruses built from AI-generated whole genomes
entries.system: Evo 1 and Evo 2 genome language models
entries.sum: The models wrote complete bacteriophage genomes modeled on ΦX174. Of nearly 300 that were synthesized, 16 produced viable phages, and a mixture of them overcame E. coli strains that resist the natural virus.
entries.open: The hit rate was about 5% on one of the smallest genomes known. Larger genomes are still out of reach.

entries.title: OpenAI model disproves an 80-year-old conjecture on the unit distance problem
entries.sum: Using algebraic number theory, the model found ways to arrange points with more pairs exactly one unit apart than the grid-like layouts long believed to be best. Outside mathematicians checked and analyzed the argument.
